content: Routine vaccination of children has proven to be a highly effective strategy for reducing the incidence of hepatitis A in the United States. Since the introduction of the hepatitis A vaccine in 1995-1996, a phased approach to childhood immunization has been implemented. This began with the 1996 recommendation by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) to vaccinate children in communities with the highest disease rates. In 1999, ACIP expanded its recommendations to include vaccination of children in states, counties, and communities with consistently elevated hepatitis A rates. These updated recommendations represent the final step in the nationwide childhood hepatitis A immunization strategy, advocating for routine vaccination of children across the country. The implementation of these recommendations strengthens existing vaccination programs, extends the benefits of hepatitis A vaccination to the entire nation, and lays the groundwork for the potential elimination of indigenous hepatitis A virus (HAV) transmission. This report updates ACIP's 1999 recommendations for hepatitis A prevention through immunization, incorporates findings from economic analyses of nationwide routine vaccination, and provides updated guidance for routine vaccination of children in the United States. Recommendations for vaccinating high-risk groups and the use of immune globulin for hepatitis A protection remain unchanged from the 1999 guidelines. Hepatitis A is caused by the hepatitis A virus (HAV), a 27-nm RNA picornavirus. It can result in either asymptomatic or symptomatic infection, with an average incubation period of 28 days (range: 15-50 days). Symptomatic illness typically begins abruptly and may include fever, malaise, anorexia, nausea, abdominal discomfort, dark urine, and jaundice. The likelihood of symptomatic infection increases with age. While most children under six years of age are asymptomatic, older children and adults are more likely to experience symptoms, with jaundice occurring in over 70% of cases. Symptoms generally last less than two months, but some individuals may experience prolonged or relapsing illness. HAV replicates in the liver, is excreted in bile, and is shed in stool. Peak infectivity occurs during the two weeks before the onset of jaundice or elevated liver enzymes, when viral concentrations in stool are highest. Viral shedding decreases after jaundice appears, but children may shed HAV for longer periods than adults, sometimes up to 10 weeks. Chronic shedding does not occur, but recurrent shedding may happen during relapses. Viremia occurs early in infection and persists through the period of liver enzyme elevation, though at much lower concentrations than in stool. Hepatitis A cannot be clinically distinguished from other types of viral hepatitis based on symptoms or epidemiologic features alone. Serologic testing for immunoglobulin M (IgM) anti-HAV is required to confirm acute HAV infection. IgM anti-HAV becomes detectable 5-10 days before symptom onset and typically declines to undetectable levels within a year. Immunoglobulin G (IgG) anti-HAV appears early in infection, remains detectable for life, and provides lifelong immunity. HAV RNA can be detected in blood and stool during the acute phase using nucleic acid amplification methods, though these techniques are primarily available in research laboratories. HAV is primarily transmitted person-to-person via the fecal-oral route. Close personal contact, particularly within households and extended family settings, is the most common mode of transmission. Children, often asymptomatic or with unrecognized infections, play a key role in HAV transmission and serve as a source of infection for others. Common-source outbreaks can also occur from exposure to fecally contaminated food or water, with uncooked foods frequently implicated. Cooked foods may transmit HAV if cooking is insufficient to inactivate the virus or if contamination occurs after cooking. Waterborne outbreaks are rare in developed countries with well-maintained sanitation and water supplies. Before the introduction of the hepatitis A vaccine, the disease was primarily cyclic, with peaks every 10-15 years. The highest incidence was among children aged 5-14 years, and young children often had asymptomatic or unrecognized infections. Certain racial/ethnic groups, such as American Indians, Alaska Natives, and Hispanics, had higher rates of hepatitis A compared to non-Hispanics. Geographic differences were also notable, with consistently elevated rates in the western and southwestern United States. The introduction of inactivated hepatitis A vaccines in 1995-1996 marked a turning point in hepatitis A prevention. Since ACIP's 1999 recommendations for routine vaccination of children in high-incidence areas, national hepatitis A rates have declined sharply. By 2004, rates among all age groups and racial/ethnic populations had become similar, and historic geographic differences in incidence had largely disappeared. The majority of recent cases have been reported from states without routine childhood vaccination recommendations. Groups at increased risk for hepatitis A include international travelers to countries with high or intermediate endemicity, men who have sex with men (MSM), users of injection and non-injection drugs, persons with clotting-factor disorders, and those with chronic liver disease. International travel remains a significant risk factor, with most travel-related cases associated with travel to Mexico or Central and South America. Outbreaks among MSM and drug users continue to occur, despite ACIP's longstanding vaccination recommendations for these groups. Foodborne outbreaks are relatively infrequent in the United States and are typically associated with contamination by an HAV-infected food handler. However, most food handlers with hepatitis A do not transmit the virus. Outbreaks linked to contaminated produce, such as green onions, have been increasingly recognized. Childcare centers have also been implicated in outbreaks, particularly before the widespread use of hepatitis A vaccine. In summary, routine hepatitis A vaccination of children has significantly reduced disease incidence in the United States, with profound changes in the epidemiology of the disease. Continued efforts to vaccinate high-risk groups and implement nationwide childhood vaccination are essential for further reducing hepatitis A transmission and achieving the goal of eliminating indigenous HAV transmission.
